gloss: To make something that did not exist before.
examples: Let's *create* a shared folder for the photos.
She *created* the logo in a single afternoon.
The new rules have *created* a lot of confusion.

gloss: To make or grow something, especially in quantity.
examples: The factory can *produce* two thousand units a day.
Last year they *produced* their first electric model.
The region is *producing* more wine than ever.
contrast: The verb is pruh-DOOS; the noun *produce*, meaning fruit and vegetables, is PROH-doos.

gloss: To make goods in a factory, in large numbers.
examples: They *manufacture* batteries in Ohio.
The chairs were *manufactured* in the 1960s.
The company stopped *manufacturing* film cameras years ago.

gloss: To build something large by putting its parts together.
examples: The city plans to *construct* a new bridge.
Workers *constructed* the stage in two days.
They are *constructing* a bike path along the river.

transitivity: both — transitive (assemble a bookshelf), intransitive (a crowd assembled)
gloss: To put the parts of something together, or to gather in one place.
examples: The desk is easy to *assemble*.
We *assembled* the grill without the instructions.
A crowd was *assembling* outside the store.

gloss: To decide how something will look and work before it is made.
examples: Who is going to *design* the cover?
She *designed* the whole kitchen herself.
This chair was *designed* for small apartments.
contrast: The *g* is silent: dih-ZYN, not dih-ZIG-n.

gloss: To work on something over time until it is finished or better.
examples: They want to *develop* a cheaper version.
The team *developed* the app in six months.
We have been *developing* the site all year.
contrast: No doubled *p*: *developed*, *developing* — the stress is on the middle syllable.

gloss: To make or think up something that has never existed.
examples: Nobody is going to *invent* a perfect machine.
He *invented* the device in his garage.
Somebody has already *invented* that.

gloss: To produce power, heat, or a result.
examples: Solar panels *generate* power even on cloudy days.
The post *generated* hundreds of comments.
The mill is *generating* its own electricity.

transitivity: both — transitive (form the dough into a ball), intransitive (ice formed on the window)
gloss: To give something a shape, or to come into existence as a shape.
examples: *Form* the dough into a ball.
Ice *formed* on the inside of the windows.
A line was *forming* at the door.

gloss: To make something carefully by hand, with skill.
examples: They *craft* every guitar by hand.
He *crafted* the table from a single oak plank.
The bowls are *crafted* in a small studio upstate.

gloss: To make a part or structure out of raw material, usually metal.
examples: The shop can *fabricate* the bracket in steel.
They *fabricated* the parts from a drawing.
The panels are being *fabricated* off-site.
contrast: About metal, *fabricate* means to make; about a story it means to invent a lie — *he fabricated the whole report*.

gloss: To start something that is meant to last, such as a company or a school.
examples: They want to *establish* a workshop downtown.
The school was *established* in 1908.
He is *establishing* a small press in his basement.

gloss: To start an organization, town, or institution.
examples: They plan to *found* a design school here.
She *founded* the studio in 2011.
The town was *founded* by a shipbuilder.
contrast: This *found — founded — founded* is regular and means to start. Do not confuse it with *found*, the past of *find*.

gloss: To put up a structure so that it stands upright.
examples: The crew will *erect* the scaffolding tomorrow.
They *erected* a tent in the backyard.
A statue has been *erected* in the square.

gloss: To press a soft material into a shape.
examples: *Mold* the clay while it is still soft.
She *molded* the handle with her thumbs.
The plastic is *molded* in one piece.
contrast: American spelling is *mold*, *molded*; British spells it *mould*, *moulded*.

gloss: To decide in advance how something will be done.
examples: Let's *plan* the layout before we buy anything.
They *planned* the addition for years.
We are *planning* to finish the deck in May.
contrast: The single *n* doubles: *plan → planned, planning*.

gloss: To make a first version of a drawing, plan, or document.
examples: I'll *draft* the plans this weekend.
She *drafted* three versions of the floor plan.
He is *drafting* the contract now.
contrast: American /æ/: DRAFT, not DRAHFT. The British spell the beer and the air current *draught*.

gloss: To draw something quickly and roughly.
examples: Can you *sketch* the idea for me?
He *sketched* the whole building on a napkin.
She was *sketching* the bridge from the far bank.

gloss: To make a small or virtual version of something in order to study it.
examples: Engineers *model* the airflow before building anything.
He *modeled* the house in clay.
They are *modeling* the new wing in 3D.
contrast: American keeps one *l*: *modeled, modeling*; British doubles it: *modelled*.

ru: намечать, набрасывать в общих чертах, обрисовать
gloss: To describe the main parts of a plan without the details.
examples: Let me *outline* the job in three steps.
She *outlined* the project at the meeting.
The stages are *outlined* on page two.

gloss: To think up a method or a clever arrangement for doing something.
examples: They had to *devise* a way to lift the beam.
He *devised* a clamp out of two boards.
A simple fix was *devised* overnight.
contrast: The verb *devise* ends in /z/; the noun *device* ends in /s/.

gloss: To put equipment in place so that it is ready to use.
examples: They can *install* the dishwasher on Friday.
We *installed* the shelves ourselves.
The software is still *installing*.
contrast: Two *l*'s all the way through: *install, installed, installing*.

gloss: To join pieces of metal by melting their edges together.
examples: He can *weld* aluminum.
The frame was *welded*, not bolted.
She is *welding* the joint right now.

gloss: To join small metal parts with melted soft metal.
examples: You have to *solder* the wire to the board.
He *soldered* the connection back together.
She was *soldering* when the power went out.
contrast: In American English the *l* is silent: SAH-dur.

gloss: To fasten something with nails.
examples: *Nail* the board to the post.
They *nailed* the sign above the door.
The trim was *nailed* in place yesterday.

gloss: To fasten something with screws, or to turn it into place.
examples: *Screw* the plate onto the wall.
He *screwed* the legs onto the table.
The bracket is *screwed* into a stud.

transitivity: both — transitive (bolt the rack to the floor), intransitive (the horse bolted)
gloss: To fasten something with bolts.
examples: We'll *bolt* the shelf to the studs.
They *bolted* the frame together in an hour.
The machine is *bolted* to the concrete floor.

gloss: To stick things together with glue.
examples: *Glue* the two halves and clamp them.
She *glued* the handle back on.
He is *gluing* the last strip of veneer.
contrast: The *e* drops before *-ing*: *glue → gluing*, not glueing.

gloss: To stick or cover something with tape.
examples: *Tape* the edges before you paint.
He *taped* the box shut.
She is *taping* the seams.

gloss: To fasten something with staples.
examples: *Staple* the pages together.
He *stapled* the insulation to the studs.
The fabric is *stapled* to the underside of the seat.

gloss: To join cloth or leather with a needle and thread.
examples: She can *stitch* the seam by hand.
They *stitched* leather straps onto the bag.
He was *stitching* a patch onto his jacket.

gloss: To make a round hole with a drill.
examples: *Drill* a small hole first.
He *drilled* four holes in the wrong place.
She is *drilling* into brick.

gloss: To hit something with a hammer, or to shape it by hitting.
examples: *Hammer* the nail flush with the board.
He *hammered* the dent out of the fender.
Someone was *hammering* upstairs all morning.

gloss: To cover a wall or ceiling with a smooth layer of plaster.
examples: They will *plaster* the ceiling next week.
The walls were *plastered* and painted.
He is *plastering* over the old cracks.

gloss: To cover a surface with tiles.
examples: We want to *tile* the bathroom floor.
They *tiled* the shower in plain white.
He is *tiling* the backsplash this weekend.

gloss: To cover a road or path with a hard surface.
examples: The city will *pave* the alley in June.
They *paved* the driveway last fall.
The road is being *paved* one lane at a time.

gloss: To put electrical wiring into a building or a device.
examples: An electrician has to *wire* the new outlets.
He *wired* the garage himself.
The house was *wired* in the 1950s.

gloss: To build the supporting structure of something, or to put it in a frame.
examples: They will *frame* the walls tomorrow.
The crew *framed* the second floor in three days.
He is *framing* the drawing for her birthday.

gloss: To cover a surface with paint, or to make a picture with paint.
examples: We should *paint* the porch before winter.
She *painted* the door a deep green.
They have *painted* the whole apartment.

gloss: To make a surface smooth by rubbing it with sandpaper.
examples: *Sand* the edges before you stain them.
He *sanded* the floor down to bare wood.
She is *sanding* the last coat smooth.

gloss: To rub a surface until it shines.
examples: *Polish* the brass with a soft cloth.
He *polished* the counter until it shone.
She is *polishing* the finished bowl.
contrast: The verb is PAH-lish; *Polish*, meaning from Poland, is POH-lish.

gloss: To put a clear hard coating on wood.
examples: *Varnish* the table after it dries.
He *varnished* the deck chairs last summer.
The wood has been *varnished* twice.

gloss: To close a gap or cover a surface so that nothing gets through.
examples: *Seal* the gap with caulk.
They *sealed* the concrete before winter.
The joints are *sealed* with silicone.

gloss: To cover a surface with a thin layer of something.
examples: *Coat* the pan with oil first.
The frame was *coated* in black enamel.
They are *coating* the pipes with rubber.

gloss: To send liquid over a surface in very small drops.
examples: *Spray* the primer in thin layers.
He *sprayed* the chairs matte black.
She is *spraying* the frame outside.
contrast: A vowel before the *y* keeps it: *sprayed, spraying* — not spraied.

gloss: To color wood with a liquid that soaks in.
examples: We'll *stain* the shelves walnut.
He *stained* the deck a dark gray.
The boards are *stained* but not sealed.

gloss: To cover something so that heat, cold, or electricity cannot pass through.
examples: They need to *insulate* the attic.
We *insulated* the crawl space last year.
The pipes are *insulated* with foam.

gloss: To make a figure by shaping clay, stone, or wax.
examples: She can *sculpt* a face in an afternoon.
He *sculpted* the figure out of wax.
The artist is *sculpting* a horse in clay.

gloss: To cut wood or stone with a chisel.
examples: *Chisel* out the waste between the lines.
He *chiseled* the joints by hand.
She is *chiseling* the date into the stone.
contrast: American keeps one *l*: *chiseled, chiseling*; British doubles it: *chiselled*.

gloss: To shape hot metal by hammering it.
examples: They still *forge* the blades by hand.
The hinges were *forged*, not cast.
He is *forging* a hook out of scrap steel.
contrast: *Forge* also means to fake a signature or a document.

gloss: To bend something over on itself.
examples: *Fold* the metal along the score line.
She *folded* the sheet into a paper box.
The legs are *folded* flat for storage.

gloss: To turn something around itself, or out of its proper shape.
examples: *Twist* the two wires together.
He *twisted* the cap off the tube.
The bracket had been *twisted* out of shape.

gloss: To make something flat, or to become flat.
examples: *Flatten* the board with a hand plane.
The press *flattened* the sheet in one pass.
He is *flattening* the seams with a roller.

gloss: To pull something so that it becomes longer or tighter.
examples: *Stretch* the canvas over the frame.
She *stretched* the fabric and stapled it down.
The screen is *stretched* tight.

gloss: To push down on something firmly, often to shape or flatten it.
examples: *Press* the veneer down hard.
The seams were *pressed* flat with an iron.
The machine is *pressing* the panels together.

gloss: To press something from two sides.
examples: *Squeeze* the tube from the bottom.
He *squeezed* the glue into the joint.
She is *squeezing* the clamp shut.

gloss: To press something so hard that it breaks into pieces or loses its shape.
examples: The mill *crushes* the stone into gravel.
The box was *crushed* in shipping.
They are *crushing* old concrete for the base.

gloss: To flatten or shape something by moving a roller over it, or to turn it into a tube.
examples: *Roll* the clay into a thin sheet.
He *rolled* the paint on in long strokes.
She is *rolling* the dough out now.

gloss: To make a blade or a point sharp.
examples: *Sharpen* the chisel before you start.
He *sharpened* every blade in the shop.
She is *sharpening* the saw teeth by hand.

gloss: To cut a small amount off something to make it neat or to make it fit.
examples: *Trim* the edge with a sharp knife.
He *trimmed* the door so it would close.
She is *trimming* the excess off the seam.
contrast: The *m* doubles: *trim → trimmed, trimming*.

gloss: To cut something with hard strokes of an axe or knife.
examples: *Chop* the boards into short lengths.
He *chopped* the kindling before dark.
She is *chopping* onions for the stew.
contrast: The *p* doubles: *chop → chopped, chopping*.

gloss: To cut something into thin flat pieces.
examples: *Slice* the veneer as thin as you can.
He *sliced* the pipe with a hacksaw.
She is *slicing* the bread now.

gloss: To fix one thing onto another.
examples: *Attach* the bracket with two screws.
He *attached* the legs to the seat.
The label is *attached* to the underside.
contrast: You attach one thing **to** another: *attach the shelf to the wall*.

gloss: To join two things so that something can pass between them.
examples: *Connect* the red wire to the terminal.
He *connected* the hose to the pump.
The two rooms are *connected* by a short hallway.
contrast: Connect one thing **to** another, or two things **with** a part.

gloss: To put two pieces together so that they become one.
examples: *Join* the boards with glue and dowels.
The pipes were *joined* with a metal collar.
He is *joining* the two halves right now.

gloss: To connect two things so that they work or move together.
examples: A short chain *links* the two gates.
They *linked* the shed to the house wiring.
The buildings are *linked* by a covered walkway.

gloss: To close or fix something firmly in place.
examples: *Fasten* the panel with four bolts.
She *fastened* the strap around the load.
The lid is *fastened* with a latch.
contrast: The *t* is silent: FAS-uhn, like *listen* and *soften*.

gloss: To make something tighter or firmer.
examples: *Tighten* the screws a quarter turn.
He *tightened* the belt until it stopped slipping.
She is *tightening* the last bolt.

gloss: To make something less tight.
examples: *Loosen* the nut before you pull the wheel.
He *loosened* the clamp too soon.
The joint has *loosened* over the years.
contrast: The *s* is /s/, not /z/: LOO-suhn. Compare *lose*, which ends in /z/.

gloss: To fix something onto a wall, a stand, or a support.
examples: *Mount* the TV at eye level.
They *mounted* the camera on a pole.
The shelf is *mounted* with hidden brackets.

gloss: To fix something firmly so that it cannot move.
examples: *Anchor* the post in concrete.
The railing was *anchored* to the deck joists.
They are *anchoring* the frame to the slab.
contrast: The *ch* is /k/: ANG-kur.

gloss: To fasten something so that it stays in place.
examples: *Secure* the load with two straps.
He *secured* the ladder to the roof rack.
The panels are *secured* with clips.

gloss: To pass something long and thin through a hole or a narrow space.
examples: *Thread* the cable through the hole.
She *threaded* the wire behind the wall.
He is *threading* the bolt into the nut.
contrast: Here *ea* is /ɛ/: THRED rhymes with *red*, not with *read* the noun.

gloss: To fasten something with a pin, or to hold it against a surface.
examples: *Pin* the pattern to the fabric.
She *pinned* the hem before sewing it.
The plan is *pinned* to the wall of the shop.
contrast: The *n* doubles: *pin → pinned, pinning*.

gloss: To hold something tightly with a clamp.
examples: *Clamp* the joint until the glue sets.
He *clamped* the board to the bench.
The pieces are *clamped* overnight.

gloss: To make something stronger by adding material or support.
examples: We should *reinforce* the shelf with a center support.
They *reinforced* the floor with steel beams.
The corners are *reinforced* with metal plates.

gloss: To make something work again after it has broken.
examples: Can you *fix* the hinge?
He *fixed* the leak with a rubber washer.
The heater is being *fixed* today.

gloss: To put something damaged back into good condition.
examples: They can *repair* the roof in a day.
The crack was *repaired* with epoxy.
He is *repairing* the fence this morning.

gloss: To repair something small, especially clothing or a tear.
examples: She can *mend* almost anything.
He *mended* the net with a loop of twine.
The sleeve has been *mended* twice.

gloss: To bring something old back to its original condition.
examples: They plan to *restore* the old mill.
He *restored* the truck over four winters.
The windows are being *restored* one at a time.

gloss: To repair and modernize a building or a room.
examples: They want to *renovate* the kitchen.
We *renovated* the upstairs bathroom last spring.
The building is being *renovated* floor by floor.

gloss: To change the structure or layout of a room or building.
examples: They are going to *remodel* the basement.
We *remodeled* the whole first floor.
The store has been *remodeled* twice since 2010.
contrast: American keeps one *l*: *remodeled, remodeling*. *Remodel* is the everyday American word where the British say *do up* or *convert*.

gloss: To replace something with a newer or better version.
examples: We should *upgrade* the wiring.
They *upgraded* the furnace last winter.
The kitchen has been fully *upgraded*.

gloss: To put a new thing where an old or broken one was.
examples: We need to *replace* the broken tile.
He *replaced* the whole panel.
Two windows are being *replaced* today.
contrast: You replace one thing **with** another, not by another.

gloss: To cover a hole with a piece of material.
examples: *Patch* the hole before you paint.
He *patched* the drywall with mesh tape.
The roof has been *patched* three times.

gloss: To change part of something so that it works differently.
examples: We can *modify* the design to fit.
They *modified* the frame to take a bigger motor.
The plans are being *modified* again.
contrast: The *-y* changes: *modifies, modified*, but *modifying* keeps it.

gloss: To change something, usually slightly.
examples: Do not *alter* the drawings without telling me.
She *altered* the jacket to fit.
The plan has been *altered* twice.
contrast: *Alter*, to change, sounds the same as *altar*, the table in a church.

gloss: To move or change something a little so that it is right.
examples: *Adjust* the hinge until the door closes.
He *adjusted* the legs to level the table.
She is *adjusting* the belt tension.

gloss: To take a machine or structure apart piece by piece.
examples: We have to *dismantle* the bed to move it.
They *dismantled* the scaffolding in an hour.
The press is being *dismantled* for parts.

gloss: To knock a building down on purpose.
examples: The city will *demolish* the old garage.
They *demolished* the wall in one morning.
The building has already been *demolished*.

gloss: To produce words or images on paper with a machine.
examples: Can you *print* two copies?
She *printed* the labels this morning.
The shop is *printing* the posters now.

gloss: To produce a book, article, or post and make it available to the public.
examples: They *publish* four books a year.
He *published* the plans online for free.
The article was *published* last week.

gloss: To cook or harden something with dry heat in an oven.
examples: *Bake* the clay at three hundred degrees.
She *baked* two loaves this morning.
The tiles are *baking* in the kiln.

gloss: To make beer, or to make coffee or tea with hot water.
examples: They *brew* their own beer in the garage.
He *brewed* a batch last weekend.
The coffee is still *brewing*.

gloss: To put substances together so that they become one.
examples: *Mix* the concrete in small batches.
He *mixed* the paint by hand.
She is *mixing* the mortar now.
contrast: A verb ending in *-x* takes *-es*: *mixes*.

gloss: To move a liquid or mixture around with a stick or spoon.
examples: *Stir* the paint before you use it.
He *stirred* the mixture until it was smooth.
She is *stirring* the glue into the sawdust.
contrast: The *r* doubles: *stir → stirred, stirring*.

gloss: To press and fold dough or clay with your hands.
examples: *Knead* the dough for ten minutes.
He *kneaded* the clay to get the air out.
She is *kneading* the bread on the counter.
contrast: The *k* is silent, so *knead* sounds exactly like *need*.

gloss: To put a product into a box or wrapper for sale or shipping.
examples: They *package* each lamp in foam.
The kits were *packaged* by hand.
We are *packaging* the last orders now.

gloss: To put things into a box, a bag, or a container.
examples: *Pack* the fragile parts separately.
He *packed* the crate with straw.
She is *packing* the tools into the van.

gloss: To put a name or a mark on something so it can be identified.
examples: *Label* every wire before you cut it.
He *labeled* the boxes by room.
The jars are *labeled* with the date.
contrast: American keeps one *l*: *labeled, labeling*; British writes *labelled*.

gloss: To give a machine or a computer a set of instructions.
examples: You can *program* the thermostat from your phone.
He *programmed* the machine to cut the same shape every time.
She is *programming* the controller tonight.
contrast: Americans write the base form *program*, but still double the *m*: *programmed, programming*.

gloss: To write the instructions that make a program work.
examples: She can *code* the whole interface herself.
He *coded* the first version in a weekend.
They are *coding* the new checkout page.

gloss: To find the size, length, or amount of something.
examples: *Measure* twice, cut once.
He *measured* the opening three times.
She is *measuring* the room for a rug.

gloss: To draw a line or sign on something to show where to cut or drill.
examples: *Mark* the studs with a pencil.
He *marked* the cut line with tape.
The centers are *marked* on the drawing.

gloss: To put two or more things in a straight line, or in the right position.
examples: *Align* the holes before you push the pin in.
He *aligned* the doors so the gaps matched.
The panels are not *aligned*.
contrast: The *g* is silent: uh-LYN.

gloss: To make a surface flat and horizontal.
examples: *Level* the base before you set the post.
They *leveled* the ground with a rake.
He is *leveling* the washer with a wrench.
contrast: American keeps one *l*: *leveled, leveling*; British writes *levelled*.

gloss: To put something in a particular place on purpose.
examples: *Position* the brace under the beam.
He *positioned* the lamp over the bench.
The speakers are *positioned* in the corners.

gloss: To put things in a particular order or pattern.
examples: *Arrange* the tiles before you glue any of them.
She *arranged* the tools on a pegboard.
He is *arranging* the chairs in a circle.

gloss: To put things one on top of another.
examples: *Stack* the boards with spacers between them.
He *stacked* the bricks along the wall.
The crates are *stacked* three high.

gloss: To supply a place or a person with the tools needed for a job.
examples: They *equip* every van with a full tool kit.
The shop was *equipped* with two lathes.
We are *equipping* the lab this month.
contrast: The *p* doubles: *equip → equipped, equipping*.

gloss: To put furniture into a room or a house.
examples: It will cost a lot to *furnish* the whole house.
They *furnished* the apartment from thrift stores.
The place was already *furnished* when we moved in.

gloss: To make something look better by adding color or ornament.
examples: Let's *decorate* the room in warm colors.
She *decorated* the cake with fresh berries.
The hall was *decorated* for the party.

gloss: To change the color of cloth, hair, or leather with a colored liquid.
examples: You can *dye* the fabric a darker blue.
She *dyed* the cotton with onion skins.
He is *dyeing* the wool in a big pot.
contrast: *Dyeing* keeps the *e*; *dying*, from *die*, does not.

gloss: To make something exactly like an original.
examples: *Copy* the pattern onto stiff paper.
He *copied* the joint from an old chair.
She is *copying* the drawing to scale.
contrast: A consonant before *-y* changes it: *copies, copied*, but *copying* keeps the *y*.

gloss: To change something so that it suits one particular person or use.
examples: You can *customize* the handles.
They *customized* the van for long trips.
Every bike is *customized* for the rider.
contrast: American spells it *-ize*; the British often write *customise*.

gloss: To make or change something so that it fits an exact need.
examples: We can *tailor* the design to your space.
He *tailored* the jacket to fit her shoulders.
The course is *tailored* to beginners.
contrast: You tailor something **to** a person or a need.

gloss: To improve something by making small careful changes.
examples: We can *refine* the shape later.
She *refined* the prototype three times.
The process has been *refined* over many years.

gloss: To make a whole by putting parts together, especially music or writing.
examples: He can *compose* a tune in an hour.
She *composed* the piece for four voices.
The image is *composed* of thousands of small tiles.

transitivity: both — transitive (harden the steel), intransitive (the glue hardened overnight)
gloss: To become hard, or to make something hard.
examples: Heat will *harden* the steel.
The resin *hardened* overnight.
The clay is *hardening* faster than we expected.

gloss: To make something stronger, or to become stronger.
examples: Two braces will *strengthen* the frame.
They *strengthened* the bridge deck last year.
The mix is *strengthening* as it cures.

gloss: To make something wider, or to become wider.
examples: They plan to *widen* the doorway.
The crew *widened* the road by six feet.
The crack is *widening* every winter.

gloss: To make something shorter.
examples: *Shorten* the legs by an inch.
He *shortened* the cord and put a new plug on it.
